title: The lotus leaf in the water
hookLine: a lotus leaf sits in the water all day and comes out dry
carry: offer every act to god; let the fruit go

lines: A LEAF IN THE POND ALL DAY.
cards: A lotus leaf spends its whole life in a pond. Rain lands on it, water laps at its edges, and still, lift it out and the surface is dry.
The Gita takes that ordinary sight and makes it the picture for a whole way of acting.

teach.h: THE LEAF STAYS IN THE WATER.
teach.b: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. The one who acts, setting every action in Brahman and letting go of attachment, isn't stained by wrongdoing, the way a lotus leaf isn't wet by water.
The leaf doesn't leave the pond or hide from the rain. It's in the water completely, and the water doesn't cling.
Chapter three starts from a plain fact: nobody can stay even a moment without acting. Even keeping the body going is action.

teach.h: CHAPTER FOUR: STILLNESS INSIDE THE WORK.
teach.b: Chapter four turns the screw: the wise see inaction in action and action in inaction. Someone can sit perfectly still and be churning inside, and someone can work all day and be at rest.

teach.h: CHAPTER FIVE: OFFER IT, AND STAY DRY.
teach.b: Then chapter five gives us the leaf. The next verses say the yogis act with body, mind and understanding, even with the senses alone, letting go of attachment, to make themselves clean.
The one who lets go of the fruit comes to a steady peace, while the one who grabs at the fruit, driven by wanting, is bound.

The commentators agree on the leaf and differ on the phrase before it: is setting an act in Brahman handing it to the Lord, as a servant works for a master, or seeing that nature, not the Self, does the work?

Many Hindu families live this verse without naming it. At the end of a puja they say an old prayer from the Bhagavata Purana: whatever I do, with body, speech, mind or senses, I offer it all to Narayana.
Some say it in one word: Krishnarpanamastu, let it be offered to Krishna.
That's karma yoga in a breath: do the work all the way, hand over the fruit, and praise or blame rolls off like water.

how: Many Hindu families close a puja by offering all their actions to God, with the Bhagavata Purana's prayer 'kayena vacha...' or simply 'Krishnarpanamastu', and teachers point to the Gita's lotus leaf when they speak about working in the world without clinging to its results.

o: work avoided so that no wrongdoing can stain you
work done fully, with nothing clinging to it
a vow to stay out of the world's business

games.q: three chapters on action — tap the pairs.
p: nobody can stay a moment without acting
inaction in action, action in inaction
the lotus leaf, in water, not wet
the one who grabs at the fruit

s: the Gita's lotus leaf stays dry by staying out of the water
the leaf is in the water completely; the water simply doesn't cling to it.
in chapter four, the wise see action in inaction and inaction in action
someone can be still and churning, or working and at rest.
the commentators agree on the leaf but argue over what setting an action in Brahman means
the picture is shared; the phrase before it is read in more than one way.

games.q: you want your work to stop weighing on you. by the Gita's chapter five, what does the lotus leaf do?
o: leaves the pond for somewhere dry.
stays in the water, and the water doesn't cling.
sinks, so the rain can't reach it.
games.why: the leaf stays in the pond. Krishna's point is acting fully while letting go of attachment, not stepping out of the work.

practice: Hold your hands open, palms up, like two leaves, and let the day's water come: a waiting task, a conversation still running in your head.
Let it land, and with each out-breath feel it bead up and roll away while the hands stay where they are.
If you pray, you can set one of today's tasks in the hands of the one you pray to as you breathe out, the way families say Krishnarpanamastu, let it be offered to Krishna.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action, the work no one can step out of. In the Gita's lotus leaf, it's work done fully, with nothing clinging to it.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: padmapatra, lotus leaf, the Gita's picture in chapter five for action that leaves no stain.

carryVoice: Your line: offer every act to God; let the fruit go. Next, a year of service, one piece at a time. That's day nine hundred sixty-eight.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.5, 3.8 (no one stays a moment without acting; even the body's upkeep is action)

Bhagavad Gita 5.10–5.12 (the lotus leaf; the yogis act to purify themselves; the unattached reach peace, the attached are bound)
